title: Each Voyager probe carries a gold plated copper phonograph record holding sounds and images chosen t
description:
Each Voyager probe carries a gold plated copper phonograph record holding sounds and images chosen to represent life and culture on Earth. The contents include 116 images, greetings in 55 languages, and a music selection running from Bach and Beethoven to Chuck Berry and Blind Willie Johnson.

The record's cover is inscribed with instructions for playing it, and a sample of pure uranium 238 so that anyone who finds it can date the launch from how much of it has decayed. Uranium 238 has a half life of about 4.5 billion years, so the clue is built to still work long after any human record of the mission is gone.

Roughly how long it will take Voyager 1 to pass within a light year and a half of another star, Gliese 445, the record's first close encounter with anything.

Producers wanted the Beatles' Here Comes the Sun on it, and the band agreed, but the record label that controlled the rights would not clear it in time. Accounts of exactly why differ in the details, so this is included as the broad, agreed shape of the story rather than a precise quote.

Humanity's message to the universe is more likely to be read by nobody for tens of thousands of years than by anybody at all.

- https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Voyager_Golden_Record: confirms both 1977 Voyager probes carry a gold plated copper record with 116 images, spoken greetings in 55 languages, natural sounds and a music selection including Bach, Beethoven, Chuck Berry and Blind Willie Johnson, describes the inscribed playback instructions and the uranium 238 sample used as a radioactive clock for dating the launch, gives Voyager 1's projected approach to within 1.6 light years of the star Gliese 445 in about 40,000 years as its first stellar encounter, and covers the disputed rights clearance story around including the Beatles' Here Comes the Sun.
